tagline: OV-099 — second operational Shuttle. Lost 73s after launch on STS-51-L (1986-01-28) with all seven crew including teacher Christa McAuliffe
dispatch: Challenger, OV-099, was the fleet's early workhorse and the site of its first catastrophe. It flew the program's first spacewalk and carried the first American woman, Sally Ride, to orbit. On 28 January 1986, launching in unusually cold weather, a rubber seal in one of its solid boosters — stiffened by the cold, a failure mode engineers had warned of — gave way, and the vehicle broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff. All seven aboard died. The disaster grounded the fleet for 32 months and exposed a management culture that had flown past a known, flagged risk.
description: Built from a structural test article (STA-099) converted to flight after Enterprise was deemed too expensive to upgrade. First flew STS-6 (1983-04-04) carrying out the first Shuttle EVA. Flew 10 missions in total: STS-6, STS-7, STS-8, STS-41-B, STS-41-C, STS-41-G, STS-51-B, STS-51-F, STS-61-A, and final flight STS-51-L. On 1986-01-28, STS-51-L launched at unprecedented cold (36 °F, about 2 °C) — the right SRB's O-rings failed to seal, hot gas from the joint breached the external tank and impinged on the strut attaching the SRB to it, and the vehicle broke apart at T+73 s, after maximum dynamic pressure, at 14 km altitude. All seven crew perished, including teacher Christa McAuliffe. NASA grounded the Shuttle for 32 months, until STS-26 on 1988-09-29; the Rogers Commission traced the loss to the booster joint and to a flawed decision to launch.
